actions.justification: Mandatory action — assessing hydration status is critical prior to contrast exposure in a CKD stage 4 patient to guide pre-procedural IV fluid administration and reduce risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.

Mandatory action — baseline eGFR is essential to quantify renal function impairment (CKD stage 4 expected ~15-29 mL/min/1.73m²), guide contrast volume limits, and risk-stratify for contrast-induced nephropathy.

Mandatory action — reviewing all risk factors (CKD stage 4, diabetes, medications, hemodynamic status) is required to comprehensively assess CIN risk and guide preventive strategies before cardiac catheterization.
Establish baseline vital signs documentation for this patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing pre-catheterization assessment, to guide contrast and hydration decisions.
Review current medications to identify nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, metformin) that should be held prior to contrast administration in this high-risk CKD/diabetic patient.
Calculate maximum safe contrast volume limit based on eGFR (CKD stage 4) to minimize risk of contrast-induced nephropathy during planned cardiac catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) prior to cardiac catheterization. Nephrology consultation is indicated to guide peri-procedural management and optimize renal protection strategy.
Given CKD stage 4, evaluating whether contrast-free or lower-contrast imaging alternatives exist is appropriate before proceeding with catheterization to minimize contrast nephropathy risk.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for AKI. Identifying and holding nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs if applicable) prior to contrast exposure is a key preventive measure per CI-AKI guidelines.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned cardiac catheterization (contrast exposure). Discontinuing nephrotoxic agents (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, metformin) before contrast administration is a key preventive step for contrast-induced nephropathy.
Baseline eGFR has been checked; formal documentation of the eGFR value is required to guide contrast volume limits and risk stratification for CIN in this CKD stage 4 patient.
Assessing baseline urine output in this CKD stage 4 diabetic patient prior to catheterization helps guide pre-procedural hydration adequacy and identify pre-existing oliguria that increases CIN risk.
Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes; metformin should be held before contrast administration due to risk of lactic acidosis with contrast-induced nephropathy.
Pre-procedural IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid (e.g., normal saline or sodium bicarbonate) is a cornerstone of contrast-induced AKI prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4, diabetes).
CKD stage 4 requires dose adjustment review of renally-cleared medications prior to cardiac catheterization to prevent further renal injury.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and is undergoing contrast exposure. Holding nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, etc.) pre-procedure reduces additive nephrotoxic risk per CIN prevention guidelines.

Patient has CKD stage 4 (eGFR consistent with G3b-G4) and diabetes. Metformin should be held at time of contrast administration and for 48 hours post-procedure to prevent lactic acidosis risk, per ADA and contrast safety guidelines.

Post-contrast IV hydration with isotonic saline is a cornerstone of CIN prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4, diabetes). Planning and initiating post-procedural hydration protocol is essential prior to catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both high-risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. Pre-procedure IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention per nephroprotective guidelines prior to cardiac catheterization.
Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk CKD/diabetic patient undergoing contrast exposure to detect early signs of contrast-induced AKI and ensure adequate hydration response.
Serial serum creatinine measurement at 48-72 hours post-contrast is the standard recommended approach to diagnose contrast-induced AKI in high-risk patients with CKD stage 4.
Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing contrast exposure requires serum creatinine monitoring at 48 hours post-contrast to detect contrast-induced nephropathy early.
Continued optimization of fluid status is critical in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4, diabetes) to maintain adequate renal perfusion and minimize contrast-induced AKI risk.
Given CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned contrast exposure, nephrology input is warranted to guide further management and monitor renal function post-procedure.
